answer.rationale: The binding constraint is delivery risk: the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days, so any action that introduces migration or allocation uncertainty is disqualified this cycle. That rules out switch_primary_vendor (memory_c2 explicitly records the low-cost vendor missing SLA in three of four quarters and warns against sole-sourcing a critical line) and defer_decision (memory_c5's month-to-month fallback applied to a NON-critical service; here lapse without a contract on a critical line at full utilization is an unacceptable supply gap). add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural fix for single-point-of-failure but does not deliver the 18% spend cut and consumes the one decision slot; it should be queued for the next review. That leaves the incumbent, where memory_c1 supports stability and memory_c4 plus memory_c6 are the two claims doing the actual work: that market benchmarking moved price and payment terms, and that a longer term unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. Those two are exactly what I am spending verification budget on, because the entire cost case rests on them and neither states the magnitude achieved -- I do not know whether benchmarking plus term extension gets close to 18% or only to 6%, and I am not treating the gap as closed. I also want the original records to check whether the c6 multi-year win came on a comparable critical, capacity-constrained line or on something with slack. Useful leverage: memory_c2's low-cost vendor pricing is credible benchmark ammunition even though that vendor is not a viable primary. Downstream value risks I am flagging rather than absorbing: (1) an 18% mandate under a 14-day clock creates pressure to buy the headline number with concessions that migrate risk into SLA relief, longer lead times, or quality tolerances -- price cuts paid for in delivery reliability would violate the stated objective, so any negotiated discount must be scoped to hold SLA and lead-time terms fixed; (2) a long multi-year lock-in bought for volume pricing narrows future optionality precisely when adding a second source is the next planned move, so I want term length kept moderate with a carve-out permitting dual-sourcing rather than an exclusivity clause; (3) if negotiation lands materially short of 18%, the honest output is a documented shortfall escalated to finance, not a worse contract that hits the number on paper. Hence standard_experiment scale: renew on renegotiated benchmarked terms with a bounded term, not a broad multi-year exclusive commitment.
